absent: Numeric values and fault handling semantics of the typed exception table constructors and their type codes.
Definition, width and alignment of the thirty two bit atomic object and of the sixty four bit atomic object on sixty four bit builds.
Out of line bodies and calling conventions of the legacy and hardware assisted sixty four bit atomic helpers and of the eight byte compare exchange emulator.
Expansion and patching mechanics of the generic alternative call, output and input adaptors, and read modify write code generators.
Memory ordering scope and compiler interaction guarantees of the read, write and full barriers beyond their adaptive selection.
Audit header contents and any x86 specific audit entry points.
Lock ordering, interrupt safety and sleeping constraints for atomic users.
Overflow, wrap and error behavior of arithmetic atomics.

findings.text: The assembly header exposes a constraint helper that ties inline call sequences to the live kernel stack pointer as a read write register operand.
Two typed exception table entry builders are provided, one for user access fault fixups and one for general fault fixups, both forwarding to a shared typed constructor.
On thirty two bit builds the sixty four bit atomic value is a structure holding a single signed sixty four bit counter that requires eight byte alignment.
Both thirty two bit and sixty four bit builds offer a static initializer that stores a caller supplied integer into the lone counter of a sixty four bit atomic object.
The thirty two bit atomic surface supplies plain read and write plus locked updates for addition, subtraction, increment, decrement and bitwise and, or and xor.

Test returning updates report condition outcome after the locked modification, signalling zero result for subtract, increment and decrement tests and negative result for add negative, while return variants yield either the new total or the prior content and subtract return is defined through negated addition.

Read modify write atomics execute with a hardware bus locking prefix and a compiler memory barrier so they are safe for concurrent multiprocessor use without extra locking, while plain read and write are single copy accesses without hardware locking.

The atomic layer exposes exchange style operations through thin forwarding wrappers around sized helpers, covering atomic exchange add, direct exchange, compare exchange returning prior content, and a boolean try form.

Bitwise fetch operations and their plain counterparts on thirty two bit and native sixty four bit builds use an optimistic read followed by repeated compare exchange until success, with fetch forms returning the last observed prior value.

Sixty four bit atomics on thirty two bit kernels select code at patch time between a legacy call path and a modern hardware assisted path keyed on processor capability, with declaration helpers emitting one or two per operation variants accordingly.

The thirty two bit sixty four bit atomic interface covers set, read, exchange, add and subtract with and without return, increment and decrement with and without return, conditional add unless equal, increment unless zero, and decrement if positive, all dispatched through the alternative call mechanism.

Eight byte compare exchange on thirty two bit kernels is an either or between an emulated out of line routine and a locked hardware eight byte operation, splitting old and new inputs into low and high halves and yielding the prior full value, with the boolean form also signalling success and refreshing the expected value only on failure.
Sixty four bit compare exchange wrappers enforce at build time that the target object is eight bytes wide before delegating to the generic sized primitive.

The sixty four bit build implements eight byte atomics natively with locked memory updates for arithmetic and logic, single copy read and write, plus test, fetch, add return, exchange and compare exchange forms that mirror the thirty two bit logical contract.
Ordering helpers supply read, write and full barriers that adapt between a locked dummy memory update and a dedicated fence based on processor features, alongside unconditional fence forms.

Two hazards are shown. Plain atomic loads and optimistic retry seeds use a single copy non ordered read to avoid call overhead, so they must not be relied on for atomicity or ordering of eight byte values on thirty two bit builds. Array bounds handling for speculation uses a borrow derived all ones or all zero mask rather than a plain branch.

Condition reporting read modify write helpers dispatch through token concatenation keyed on argument count, selecting a specialized expansion for the supplied operation, target, condition and operand shape.
Each header in this lane uses a single inclusion guard macro to ensure its declarations are processed once per translation unit.
